publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our main result is that log-volatility behaves essentially as a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H of order 0.1, at any reasonable time scale.

span.label: smoothness (roughness) of the volatility process
span.quote: Estimating volatility from recent high frequency data, we revisit the question of the smoothness of the volatility process.

span.label: observational-study
span.quote: We now proceed to estimate the smoothness parameter sq for each q by computing the m(q, ∆) for different values of ∆ and regressing log m(q, ∆) against log ∆.

span.label: the scaling result is established at usual observation time scales
span.quote: at least at usual time scales of observation

span.label: Smoothness estimates based on whole-trading-day realized variance are expected to be biased upwards because integration smooths the process.
span.quote: Since these estimates of integrated variance are for the whole trading day, we expect estimates of the smoothness of the volatility process to be biased upwards, integration being a regularizing operation.

span.label: Volatility is never observed directly, so the key quantity m(q, Δ) can only be computed from proxies.
span.quote: Of course, the volatility process is not directly observable, and an exact computation of m(q, ∆) is not possible in practice.

span.label: The paper only treats the volatility time series; whether the model is consistent with observed option prices is deferred.
span.quote: A more detailed analysis of the consistency of our model with option prices is left for a future article.

span.label: The property cannot be estimated without first assuming the functional form whose presence is at issue.
span.quote: Indeed, meaningful results can probably only be obtained under such a specification, since it is not possible to estimate the asymptotic behavior of the covariance function without assuming a specific form

span.label: As the term is now defined, the field's central question about volatility cannot be answered at all.
span.quote: that when stated in term of the asymptotic behavior of the autocorrelation function, the long memory question can simply not be answered

span.label: Standard procedures report the property in data generated by a model that does not have it, which the authors offer as the reason the field accepted it as a stylized fact.
span.quote: Our main finding is that although the RFSV model does not have any long memory property, classical statistical procedures aiming at detecting volatility persistence tend to conclude the presence of long memory in data generated from it. This sheds new light on the supposed long memory in the volatility of financial data

span.label: long memory - SENSE 1, THE ORIGINAL AND LOOSE ONE: slow decay of the autocorrelation function, meaning anything slower than exponential
span.quote: Initially, it appears that the term long memory referred to the slow decay of the autocorrelation function (of absolute returns for example), anything slower than exponential

span.label: long memory - SENSE 2, THE LATER TECHNICAL ONE the field drifted to: a non-integrable autocorrelation function, more precisely one decaying as a power law with exponent below 1, and the recent literature assumes this sense
span.quote: Over time however, it seems that this term has acquired the more precise meaning that the autocorrelation function is not integrable, see [8], and even more precisely that it decays as a power-law with exponent less than 1. Much of the more recent literature, for example [7, 11, 13], assumes long memory in volatility in this more technical sense

span.label: volatility - AS A PROXY, ALWAYS: the process is not directly observable, so every quantity here is computed from an estimated daily stand-in taken at a fixed time of day
span.quote: Of course, the volatility process is not directly observable, and an exact computation of m(q, ∆) is not possible in practice. We must therefore proxy spot volatility values by appropriate estimated values

span.label: builds-on → fractional Brownian motion (from mathematics/physics)
span.quote: log-volatility behaves essentially as a fractional Brownian motion

span.label: builds-on → the fractional stochastic volatility (FSV) model of Comte and Renault [16]
span.quote: This leads us to adopt the fractional stochastic volatility (FSV) model of Comte and Renault [16].

span.label: extends → the FSV model of Comte and Renault [16], modified to H < 1/2
span.quote: We call our model Rough FSV (RFSV) to underline that, in contrast to FSV, H < 1/2.

span.label: contradicts → the accepted stylized fact of power-law long memory in volatility
span.quote: Once again, our conclusion is that although the (log-)volatility may exhibit some form of persistence, it does not present any long memory in the classical power law sense.

span.label: replicates → the stylized fact of near-Gaussian log-volatility increments reported by Andersen et al. ([2], [3])
span.quote: That the distribution of increments of logvolatility is close to Gaussian is a well-established stylized fact reported for example in the papers [2] and [3] of Andersen et al.

span.label: builds-on → Fukasawa [25] on the ATM volatility skew generated by fBM-driven volatility
span.quote: As already shown by Fukasawa [25], such a model with a small H reproduces the observed decay of at-the-money volatility skew with respect to time to expiry, asymptotically for short times.

span.label: long memory —operationalised-as→ Hurst parameter
span.quote: Note that in the case of the fBM, there is a one to one correspondence between regularity and long memory through the Hurst parameter

span.label: spot volatility —operationalised-as→ realized volatility
span.quote: we proxy daily spot variances by daily realized variance estimates from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance Realized Library

span.label: H ≈ 0.1 — Hurst exponent of log-volatility (H<1/2 means rough)
span.quote: log-volatility behaves essentially as a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H of order 0.1

span.label: H = 1/2 — the classical Brownian-motion boundary case
span.quote: For H = 1/2, we retrieve the classical Brownian motion.

span.label: Although volatility is NOT long-memory under RFSV, classical persistence tests spuriously detect long memory in RFSV-generated data — explaining why long memory became an accepted stylized fact.
span.quote: classical statistical procedures aiming at detecting volatility persistence tend to conclude the presence of long memory in data generated from it. This sheds light on why long memory of volatility has been widely accepted as a stylized fact.
